narrative:
The prediction that led to your denial is not a certainty, but it is a clear warning: the model estimates a 51% chance that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. Because that is slightly above the 50/50 mark, the model treated failure as more likely than success, and the admissions decision was based on that risk.

The strongest factor was your LSAT score. With a score of 23, you are far below the average of 37 among admitted students, and this difference pushed your prediction strongly toward failure. In simple terms, this evidence outweighed other parts of your record and was the main reason the risk was not lower.

Your family income was the second most important factor, but it worked in your favor. Although lower-middle-income students make up a small share of admitted applicants, the model associated your particular income background with a slightly lower likelihood of failing—so this factor nudged your prediction toward passing, not failing.

Your first-year academic standing also helped you. You ranked in the 4th decile, which is better than the 6th-decile average among accepted students. Being higher in that ranking pushed the prediction toward passing, which shows the model did recognize your early academic strength.

The path forward is clear: your LSAT score is the largest obstacle. Retaking the LSAT and improving it substantially would make the biggest difference. Strengthening your overall academic record before reapplying could also improve your chances, but the LSAT is where you have the most room to change the model’s conclusion.
